title: Twins All-Star Byron Buxton exits game with right hip discomfort
content:
WEST SACRAMENTO, Calif. — After Minnesota Twins outfielder Byron Buxton exited Tuesday night’s 4-2 loss to the Athletics with right hip discomfort, the team is in wait-and-see mode while its fanbase is hysterical about top prospect Walker Jenkins.

Buxton, who twice already this season has landed on the injured list with right hip soreness, couldn’t track down Henry Bolte’s extra-base hit to the gap and immediately slowed down after the ball went under his glove.

Twins manager Derek Shelton and an athletic trainer quickly tended to Buxton, who walked off the field under his own power after a brief delay.

After the game, Shelton was trying to piece together information about his three-time All-Star’s health. Shelton said the team previously planned to sit Buxton on Wednesday night to afford him two days of rest before the club starts a stretch of 15 straight games against American League Central opponents.

“(Buxton is) just too important to us,” Shelton said. “So we’ll see how he reports (Wednesday). Fortunately it is a night game. It’s not a quick turnaround and we do have some time.”

Though he didn’t go on the injured list until July, Buxton’s hip injury has bothered him since mid-May. He missed the All-Star Game and the start of the second half to get healthy, returning to action July 20.

But only eight days later, Buxton was removed from a game and eventually placed on the IL again, missing 14 games after receiving a shot in his hip.

Entering Tuesday’s game, Buxton was hitting .180/.286/.213 in 17 second-half games with only two extra-base hits in 70 plate appearances. He hasn’t homered since June 22, a span of 104 plate appearances.

Losing Buxton again with only 29 games remaining would be worrisome for the Twins, who are hanging on the edge of the American League wild-card race. The Twins began Tuesday two games back of the final spot.

If Buxton needs another IL stint, the Twins could turn to Jenkins, whom The Athletic’s Keith Law ranked the No. 16 prospect in baseball in May.

Finally displaying the power the Twins hoped to see, Jenkins has homered seven times in August for Triple-A St. Paul, including three multihomer games. After going 1-for-4 with a walk Tuesday, Jenkins is batting .406/.488/.768 with 12 RBIs, 11 walks and 13 strikeouts in August.

For now, the Twins must first see how Buxton responds.

“He’s been dealing with the hip issue, which we know,” Shelton said. “It kind of caught when he went to stop on the ball. … We need to make sure that we get a look at it.”

Earlier in the game, Taj Bradley produced what appears to be the first immaculate inning in Twins history. Starting with the bottom of the Athletics’ order, Bradley struck out three batters on nine pitches in the fifth inning. He threw two four-seam fastballs for strikes before Carlos Cortes chased a split-fingered fastball for strike three.

No. 9 hitter Brian Serven swung at all three pitches from Bradley: a cut fastball, a four-seamer and a curve. Bradley then completed the feat with three called strikes against Athletics leadoff hitter Bolte. The right-hander threw a cutter, splitter and a four-seamer to ring up Bolte.

“On the last pitch that’s why I called a fastball because I was like ‘F— it, best pitch,'” Twins catcher Victor Caratini said. “He threw like 100 (mph), and the batter was frozen. That’s pretty nice.”

Entering Tuesday, there had been 122 immaculate innings completed in Major League Baseball history. The Twins participated in one earlier this season when Cleveland’s Gavin Williams mowed them down on July 23. Chicago White Sox reliever Michael Kopech was immaculate against the Twins on July 10, 2024.

Bradley entered Tuesday’s game striking out 10.1 batters per nine innings this season. Working with a nasty four-pitch mix, Bradley struck out six over four innings before achieving the feat in the fifth.

Unfortunately for the Twins, the Athletics took advantage of Bradley’s few mistakes to support their pitcher, Gage Jump, who put together a spectacular outing of his own.

Bradley left a 1-2 cutter up to Cortes in the second inning that the outfielder hit for a two-run home run. The Athletics scored twice more in the sixth inning on three consecutive hits.

Bradley allowed four earned runs and seven hits, walking one and striking out 11 in 6 2/3 innings.

“Maybe the score doesn’t look that way, but he threw the ball really good,” Caratini said. “He attacked the zone when he needed to attack the zone. I’m happy for his outing. I know he doesn’t want to give up four runs, but you see the process, and it’s really, really good. Bad swings. Ahead of almost everybody. … I think it’s a really, really good start.”

Jump commanded all of his pitches, and the Twins struggled to put anything together.

Early on, the Athletics left-hander landed enough pitches in the zone with his four-seam fastball and slider for called strikes that the Twins eventually began chasing ones off the plate. Jump, who entered issuing 4.4 walks per nine innings this season, limited the Twins to two free passes.

He didn’t allow a hit until Royce Lewis’s popup fell untouched on the infield with two outs in the fourth inning. Jump then didn’t allow another until Lewis led off the seventh with a sharp liner.

The Twins chased Jump after a Kaelen Culpepper double in the seventh, but couldn’t rally the whole way.

“He executed pitches behind in counts,” Twins designated hitter Ryan Jeffers said. “He was throwing behind-count off-speed in good locations. He was really good. … This time of year is the grind. You get into August, season starts feeling heavy, feeling longer. But then once you flip into September, you get that jolt of energy, the life gets breathed back into everything.”
